title: The object of an action: biernik
goal: Change a noun when it becomes the object of an action — *-ę* for feminine words, *-a* for male living beings, and no change at all for the rest.
bekal: recognize which nouns **don't** change at all
adjust an adjective attached to the object

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Mam kota
dialogs.intro: Late afternoon on the dorm balcony. Ania shows a photo of her dog; Budi pulls up a photo of his cat.

lines.speaker: Ania:
lines.id: Do you have a pet at home?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Mam kota. Nazywa się Oyen. A ty?
lines.id: I have a cat. His name is Oyen. And you?
lines.literal: I-have cat. names self Oyen. and you?

lines.speaker: Ania:
lines.text: Mam psa i dwa koty. Kocham zwierzęta.
lines.id: I have a dog and two cats. I love animals.
lines.literal: I-have dog and two cats. I-love animals.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Kto karmi psa, kiedy jesteś w szkole?
lines.id: Who feeds the dog when you're at school?
lines.literal: who feeds dog, when you-are at school?

lines.speaker: Ania:
lines.id: My mom. She has time in the morning.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Rozumiem. Ja piję kawę rano, a siostra pije herbatę.
lines.id: I see. I drink coffee in the morning, and my sister drinks tea.
lines.literal: I-understand. I drink coffee morning, and sister drinks tea.

lines.speaker: Ania:
lines.text: Ja też lubię kawę, ale wolę herbatę wieczorem.
lines.id: I like coffee too, but in the evening I prefer tea.
lines.literal: I also like coffee, but prefer tea evening.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: Do you know that café next to the university?

lines.speaker: Ania:
lines.text: Znam. Mają dobrą kawę i tanie ciasto.
lines.id: I do. They have good coffee and cheap cake.
lines.literal: I-know. they-have good coffee and cheap cake.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: To idziemy tam jutro? Stawiam kawę.
lines.id: So shall we go there tomorrow? Coffee's on me.
lines.literal: so we-go there tomorrow? I-stand coffee.

lines.speaker: Ania:
lines.id: Sure! I'll have a large cappuccino.

notes: **Kawa becomes kawę, herbata becomes herbatę.** A feminine noun ending in *-a* changes to *-ę* when it becomes the **object** of an action. This is the ending you've seen wandering around since Unit 4 (*gazetę*, *aplikację*, *kolację*), and now it gets its name: *biernik*.

**Kot becomes kota, pies becomes psa.** **Living** masculine nouns — people and animals — get the ending *-a*. Notice *pies → psa*: the *e* inside the word disappears. A small group of words does this (*pies*, *chłopiec*, *ojciec*); there are few of them, and you can learn them as you meet them.

**Masculine nouns that aren't living beings DON'T change.** *Mam telefon*, *mam samochód*, *piję sok* — exactly the same as the dictionary form. A big saving beginners rarely notice: half of all masculine nouns need nothing done to them.
**Neuter nouns don't change either.** *Mam zwierzę*, *kupuję piwo*, *lubię ciasto*. The friendliest group of all.

**Dobra kawa becomes dobrą kawę.** The adjective changes along with its noun. For feminine words, the ending *-a* becomes **-ą**. Remember: adjective and noun always walk hand in hand; if one changes, so does the other.

**Tę kawiarnię** — the *biernik* form of *ta*. Pointing words follow the rule too: *ten → ten/tego*, *ta → tę*, *to → to*. In everyday speech many Poles say *tą* instead of *tę*; the correct written form is still *tę*.

**Kto karmi psa?** This sentence has a subject (*kto*) and an object (*psa*), and what tells them apart is not word order but **the endings**. That's why Polish can shuffle word order freely without losing the meaning — something English can't do ("dog bites man" vs "man bites dog").
**Stawiam kawę** — "coffee's on me", literally "I stand coffee". A fixed expression; don't take it apart.

grammars.title: Biernik — the object ending
body: The form that answers *kogo? co?* — whom/what the action is done to. It's the second most used form after the dictionary form.
after: In short, there are just three lines to remember: **feminine → -ę**, **masculine living → -a**, **everything else stays the same**. Two of the three groups ask nothing of you.
Feminine words ending in a consonant (*noc*, *rzecz*, *miłość*) don't change either — a small, pleasant group.
⚠️ Don't be fooled by the sound: final *-ę* is read as a **plain e**. *Kawę* is read **KA-veh**, not "ka-ven".

grammars.title: Verbs that take biernik
body: Not every verb uses this form, but almost all of the most common everyday ones do.
after: ⚠️ **One big trap awaits in Unit 14:** as soon as the sentence is negated, the object moves into a different form. *Mam kawę* → *Nie mam kawy*. *Lubię herbatę* → *Nie lubię herbaty*. Recognize the symptom now; the rule comes later.

Some verbs do **not** use *biernik* and require another form: *słuchać* (*słucham muzyki*), *szukać* (*szukam klucza*), *pomagać* (*pomagam mamie*). Learn them together with their examples, never on their own.

sections.title: Eye training: one word, two forms

blocks.text: Read each line out loud twice. What you're training is not memorizing rules but an ear that starts to feel something is off when the ending is wrong.

blocks.title: How to check yourself
items: Ask your sentence: **who/what is doing it?** That's the dictionary form. **Who/what is it done to?** That's *biernik*.
If the noun ends in *-a* and it's the one the action is done to, change it to *-ę*. That one change covers most beginner mistakes.
If it's masculine and alive, add *-a*. If it's neither — leave it alone.

blocks.title: Sentences you can use right away
items: *Piję kawę bez cukru.* — I drink coffee without sugar.
*Nie jem mięsa.* — I don't eat meat. (note: negated, so the ending is different again)
*Lubię polskie jedzenie.* — I like Polish food.
